Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control
I try to erase the memory of the event

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
The world is a dangerous place
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: For a 78-year-old woman whose index trauma is a natural disaster, this trigger is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other triggers, appraisals, memory items, and strategies all fit disaster-related loss/danger themes, but 'being looked at sexually' implies a sexual-threat/sexual-trauma context that is not represented anywhere else in the formulation or item set. This is more than unusual; it introduces a qualitatively different trauma meaning network without supporting items in Threat, Memory, Appraisals, or Strategies.

vignette:
Eleanor has been a graphic designer for fifty years, and for most of that time, her home studio was a sanctuary of controlled, creative chaos. Now, at seventy-eight, it is a sterile, silent room. Six months ago, Hurricane Ida turned her world inside out, and she has been trying to put it back in order ever since. The storm had been an abstraction on the news until it was a physical monster trying to tear its way into her house. She and her husband, George, had stayed, certain they could ride it out like they had so many others. But this was different. The sound she remembers most, the one that lives in her ears still, was not the wind, but the violent, percussive slam of the back patio door as the frame splintered and the storm surge burst into their home. It slammed open, then shut, then open again, a frantic, splintering drumbeat against the roar of the water. With the flood came the smell of the marsh and something else, sharp and cloying-the contents of their liquor cabinet, shattered and mingling with the brackish water.

In the immediate aftermath, there was only shock. But as the weeks turned into months, the storm receded from the headlines but embedded itself in her nervous system. The sound of a door closing is no longer benign. When George comes home and shuts the front door, the solid click sends a jolt of pure terror through her. For a split second, she is not in her newly renovated hallway but back in the dark, water rising around her ankles, the memory so vivid it feels like it is happening right now, not something that is over. She can feel the cold water, smell the spilled gin. As soon as the image of the splintering door floods her mind, she has a frantic, practiced response: she forces herself to visualize a blank white canvas, the kind she used to stretch for painting, and mentally chants the names of design fonts-Arial, Helvetica, Times New Roman-a dull, meaningless litany to drown out the roar of the water. She believes if she can just stop the memory before it fully forms, she can keep it from taking over. Other times, when she tries to explain this to George, the story comes out flat and distant. She can recite the events-the water level, the sound of their neighbor screaming for help, the long night waiting for rescue-with a profound numbness, as if she's recounting a film she once saw about a stranger's misfortune. It feels so extreme, so cinematic, that it's hard for her to believe it actually happened to her.

Her life has become a series of strategic retreats. She spends hours at her computer, ostensibly working on a freelance logo design, but finds herself trapped in a loop, dwelling on how it all could have been prevented. If only they had left when the first warnings came. If only they had reinforced that back door. The thoughts circle endlessly, offering no comfort, only a confirmation of her own failure to protect them. This rumination is a constant, humming background noise to her days. To quiet it, she cleans. She organises her design software folders into labyrinthine sub-folders, wipes down her monitor and keyboard repeatedly, and arranges her pens by colour, then by size, then by colour again. This compulsive tidying is the only way she can exert a small measure of control over a world that now feels utterly, terrifyingly random and dangerous. She has come to believe that safety is an illusion. For seventy-eight years, she had believed in a certain kind of order, a fundamental fairness to the world. That belief has been completely destroyed, leaving a deep, unshakeable sense of injustice in its place. What happened was senseless and cruel, and nothing has been done to make it right.

The triggers are everywhere. The smell of alcohol is one of the worst. George has taken to drinking his nightly glass of bourbon on the porch, even in the cold, after she fled the living room one evening, gasping for air, because the scent transported her back to the flood. She avoids the news, clicking the television off the moment a reporter begins a story about loss or grief, the subject matter a raw nerve. These small avoidances have accumulated, carving out canyons between her and George, and between her and the world. It was after a particularly bad night, when the slam of a kitchen cabinet sent her into a full-blown panic where she crouched in the corner of her studio, that George insisted she seek help. Eleanor agreed, not because she believed it would work, but because she was exhausted from the constant effort of pushing the memory away. She is afraid she is losing her mind, that the storm didn't just take her sense of security, but her very self. More than anything, she just wants to feel at home in her own house again, to believe that when a door closes, it is simply a door closing, and not the end of the world.
